draft.title: Torque and equilibrium
card: Torque is the turning effect of a force about a pivot. Torque = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot, so its unit is the newton metre (N m).
Only the distance measured at right angles to the line of the force counts. A bigger force or a longer distance gives a bigger torque.

A torque can turn an object clockwise or anticlockwise. A structure is in equilibrium when the forces balance (net force is zero) and the torques balance (clockwise torque equals anticlockwise torque).
Balanced torques mean the object does not start to rotate. Balanced forces mean it does not start to accelerate in a straight line. Both conditions must hold.
draft.remember: Torque = force × perpendicular distance. Equilibrium needs balanced forces and balanced torques.

a.q: Why is a door easier to push open at the handle than near the hinges?
opts: A longer distance from the pivot gives a larger torque
A longer distance from the pivot gives a larger net force
The push has a smaller size when applied near the hinges
The handle is lighter, so it needs less torque to turn
a.why: The hinges are the pivot. The same force applied further away has a larger perpendicular distance, so the torque is larger. The size of the force does not change, and torque is not the same as net force.
a.clue: The hinges are the pivot. What changes when you push further from it?

b.q: A 30 N child sits 2.0 m from the pivot of a see-saw. A second child sits on the other side. The see-saw stays level. If the second child weighs 20 N, how far from the pivot do they sit?
b.why: For torques to balance, 30 × 2.0 = 20 × d, so d = 3.0 m. The lighter child must sit further away. Sitting at 2.0 m would give a smaller torque, so the see-saw would tip toward the heavier child.
b.clue: Set the clockwise torque equal to the anticlockwise torque.

a.best: A longer distance from the pivot gives a larger torque
